I start with the cheapest thing that could work and only pay more when it fails.

1. Finding LinkedIn profiles for 206 names: Exa returned a profile for 204, Serper for 150. Where both agreed (125) it was the right person 87% of the time. Now I run both and keep the agreements. About $0.006 a person.

2. FullEnrich mobile hit rate was 78% on a list with a LinkedIn URL on every row, around 50% on lists without. Estimating one run from the other would be out by more than half. So I price every run from a sample of the actual list.

3. To list a website's pages, the Wayback Machine's index returned 2.3x what the sitemap did, for free, and it works on sites that block scraping.

4. Blitz is flat rate and unlimited for me, so it's effectively free at the margin. I try it before any per-unit tool.

The before
1. The usual way to build a TAM: filter ZoomInfo or Apollo by industry code and headcount, export.
2. A sales leader told me they were dreading the question "why are we paying $40K a year for ZoomInfo".
3. A headcount field can't tell you how many dentists work at a two-chair practice.

The build (Australian dental, client unnamed)
4. I stacked the free lists: open map data, Google listings, the dental association's register, a booking platform's public practitioner rosters, every practice's own website, and the Wayback Machine for practice sites that no longer load.
5. I read each source's terms before pulling from it. Several were ruled out on their own terms, including Google's own Places API.
6. The association register listed one big chain at 6 locations. Its own website lists 171.
7. I sized each practice by counting named clinicians on its own team page or booking roster, and checked every name against the page in code. A model saying "12 dentists" was wrong far more often than a list of names checked against the page.
8. Two cheap AI models read 6,818 practice websites for $16.40. The same job run as Claude agents worked out at about $3,397.
9. I drew a blind answer key before counting and scored the build against it.
10. A page I couldn't read is marked unread, never "no dentists here".
11. Result: about 10,500 businesses, 14,000 locations, 25,000 named clinicians and 5,600 decision makers.
12. The regulator counts 29,119 registered dental practitioners. I used that as a sanity check on the total, not as the number itself.

Cost and time
13. Paid spend I can trace across the whole build comes to roughly $30 to $35, plus a flat subscription for the decision-maker lookups. (This is an estimate pieced together from the run notes, not a reconciled ledger.)
14. First build was 26 Aug and the fifth draft landed 15 Oct: seven weeks over five drafts. It's cheap in money and expensive in hours, and ZoomInfo is the reverse.

The how-to for any industry
15. Start from the regulator's or licensing body's count, so you know roughly what complete looks like.
16. Stack every free list your industry has: map data, the association register, booking or scheduling platforms with public pages, government registers.
17. Count each chain from its own website's location list, not from a register.
18. Size businesses by named people on their own pages, not by a headcount estimate.
19. Check a small sample by hand before you count anything, then score yourself against it.
20. Use cheap models for the reading, and check every name they return against the page.
21. Use the Wayback Machine for dead sites.

- Result: about 10,500 businesses, 14,000 locations, 25,000 named clinicians and 5,600 decision makers.

[Facts from Josh's own project records, read back to Josh on 20 October 2026 with "keep or cut whatever you like". He kept all of them:]
Who releases them (US public bodies, from the widest run of 2,390 boards): school districts, utilities and transit, universities, pension systems, counties, cities, public hospitals.
Where you find them: each board's own website and archive pages, the board portals they post to, links inside agenda PDFs, councils' meeting systems (one has a free data feed), meeting video captions and news coverage.
What's in them: current-year audit plans, audit findings and risk reports, all dated.
What we were hunting: one specific risk named in an audit plan.
The noise, from one run: 43,789 papers read across 1,541 boards. 106 organisations qualified on the first pass, and 52 held up. 28 were "vendor management" that meant towing contracts, golf concessions and ambulance response times. 9 were the wrong government, including three Springfields and two Orange Counties. One county had posted 21,184 papers, so we capped each government at 150. That run finished at 63 accounts.
Once, 604 boards came back "nothing found" because the reader had failed: 338 of 368 batches were never read.

[Claude's take on each method. Written by Claude from Josh's notes above and from his own builds, then shown to Josh in full on 26 Oct 2026 for him to review and correct]
8 ways to detect what software a company runs
(3 of which hardly anyone in go-to-market uses).

Website code
→ Most tools leave a script or tag in the site's code.
→ Pro: cheap, and the best fit for customer-facing tools.
→ I get it free while scraping practice sites for decision makers.
→ One build found 915 booking systems across 1,933 sites.
→ Con: it only sees the website. Back-office tools stay invisible.
→ Vendors: BuiltWith, Wappalyzer.
→ Effort to use: easy. Used in GTM: everywhere.

Job ads
→ Ads list the tools candidates need to know.
→ Pro: it picks up back-office tools that never touch the website.
→ Con: it's inferred. The ad might be old, or name the tool they're leaving.
→ Vendors: TheirStack, PredictLeads.
→ Effort to use: easy. Used in GTM: everywhere.

The vendor's own proof
→ Customer logos and case studies on the vendor's site.
→ Pro: rarely wrong. A few vendors publish a finder that lists every customer.
→ Con: usually small numbers, and only the happy customers.
→ Effort to use: easy. Used in GTM: often.

Their integration and privacy pages
→ Companies name the tools they plug into.
→ Privacy policies often list the suppliers that touch customer data.
→ Pro: the best evidence there is, because they wrote it.
→ Con: most never say, and it means reading a lot of pages.
→ Effort to use: medium, nobody sells it. Used in GTM: sometimes.

DNS records
→ Every domain publishes where its email goes and which apps it verified.
→ Pro: someone had to set each record up, so it's hard to fake.
→ Strongest on email and security tools.
→ Con: no proof of live use. Old records outlive the tool.
→ Vendors: SecurityTrails, WhoisXML.
→ Effort to use: hard. Used in GTM: rarely.

Network banners
→ Scanners check every server online and log what software answers.
→ Pro: it finds the firewall or VPN nothing else can see.
→ Con: hard to tie a server to a company. No proof of live use.
→ Vendors: Censys.
→ Effort to use: hard. Used in GTM: barely.

Login portals
→ Some tools give each customer their own address, like acme.vendor.com.
→ Pro: close to a yes or no. The portal exists or it doesn't.
→ Con: only works for tools built that way.
→ Some answer for any name you make up, so test a fake one first.
→ Effort to use: hard, you build it. Used in GTM: barely.

Password reset checks
→ Put a work email into a tool's "forgot password" page.
→ Plenty of tools answer differently when the account exists.
→ Pro: it confirms a named person has an account.
→ Con: one email at a time, and that person may get a reset email.
→ Effort to use: hard, you build it. Used in GTM: barely.

Which one I reach for depends on how the software shows up.
Usually it's a few.

On one build we checked against a list of known customers.
No single method found more than 43% of them. Together they found 54%.
Nearly half didn't show up anywhere.

So when a tool shows up through two of these, I trust it more.

THE FINDINGS JOSH APPROVED AS THE SOURCE MATERIAL FOR THIS POST (written up by Claude from Josh's own recount run on 27 October 2026; Josh asked for the draft on this basis):

What happened: Josh started from a downloaded dataset of 21,783 US sales teams whose role counts looked wrong. Managers outnumbered reps at a lot of companies and SDRs looked undercounted. Rather than throw the SDR question away, he recounted it. In a 20-company test, the file's 2,700 "managers" turned out to be mostly account managers (1,055), directors and above (475) and business development managers (290). Front-line sales managers were 443. The file found SDRs at 8 of the 20 companies; LinkedIn showed 14.

The recount: every US employee on LinkedIn was pulled for 2,224 US software companies, and title searches were run for the 179 largest. Every job title was sorted into a role. A 420-title answer key was labelled blind by a separate checker, and the sorting agreed with it on 94% of people in the roles that matter. Net-new sellers means reps plus business development managers. Account managers, renewals and account directors are left out because they work existing customers.

The finding: 2,206 US software companies with at least 5 net-new sellers. 89,697 net-new sellers. 12,314 SDRs.

Net-new sellers per SDR, by company size:
51 to 200 employees: 4.8
201 to 500 employees: 4.7
501 to 1,000 employees: 4.6
1,001 to 5,000 employees: 6.2
5,001 to 10,000 employees: 10.0
10,000+ employees: 14.2

Below 1,000 employees it sits at about one SDR per 4.7 sellers in every size band. Above that, SDR coverage falls to a third.

It holds when each band's 10 biggest teams are removed: 4.6, 4.4, 4.5, 5.6, 10.0. Even if every inside sales rep at the 5,000+ companies were really an SDR, that band would only fall to 7.7.

70% of these companies have at least one US SDR. The original file said 47%.

What it cannot say is why. Only US profiles are counted, so SDR teams based overseas do not show up, which may explain part of the drop. More inbound demand, or account executives prospecting their own named accounts, are other possibilities. None of these was checked.

Limits: US LinkedIn profiles only, one company page per company, roles sorted by job title, October 2026.
